uncited: Adaptive Ray Sampling refers to a family of techniques in volume rendering and neural radiance fields (NeRF) that dynamically adjust the number, distribution, or density of samples along rays to optimize the trade-off between computational cost and visual fidelity.

Unlike uniform sampling, which casts a fixed number of samples regardless of scene complexity, these methods use metrics such as rendering error, density, or spatial coherence to concentrate samples in complex regions (e.g., high-frequency details, surfaces) and reduce them in empty or smooth areas.

This family is distinct from [Resolution Adaptation](3063-resolution-adaptation.md) (which adjusts pixel resolution) and [Temporal and Progressive Rendering](11267-temporal-and-progressive-rendering.md) (which leverages temporal coherence), focusing instead on spatial and structural adaptivity within the ray-marching process itself.
Adaptive sampling in volume rendering originated from the need to handle the high computational cost of ray marching through dense volumetric data.

In the context of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), the seminal work on hierarchical sampling [S4, unofficial][S5, unofficial] established the two-stage coarse-to-fine approach as a standard for improving detail without uniform dense sampling.
